published_title: THE VOTE OF THE UPLIFTED GOATS

story.title: THE VOTE OF THE UPLIFTED GOATS
story.deck: Forty goats in a dale byre have voted, unanimously, for something nobody can name, and a sale is about to fence off the hill; Illuminara spends two evenings in the straw until she hears what the vote is a translation of, and lets the herd correct her answer.
story.shape: Seven scenes across eleven days: a byre meeting, a bedtime counting game, a back room of the dale registry, a correction in the straw, a conversation at a pasture gate, a dawn climb with the whole herd, and the sitting of the assembly.

scenes.title: The Byre
paragraphs: *Marrick Farm, Brannoch Dale · evening, eleven days before the sitting*

The goats had called the meeting, and Odile Marrick wanted that understood before anything else. They had called it by walking into the byre at dusk, all forty, and standing in the straw in the patient way of animals who have listened to people for a long time. A veterinary trial that went wrong eleven years ago had left them able to follow an argument. It had not left them quick about it.

**Odile**  
They voted last Tuesday. Forty on the left side of the byre, and then eleven walked across to the right and back again, and the vet wrote that down as a recount. I think it was a joke.

**Illuminara**  
What did they vote for?
Odile held out the vet's notepad. It carried three phrases, copied down over three nights: *the hill*, *the count*, *the going-up*.

**Odile**  
The assembly sits in eleven days to decide whether they are livestock or residents. A Mr Pruett is arranging to sell the high pasture to people who want to put cabins on it. I have been asked to bring the goats' position, and I do not have one. I have three phrases.

**Illuminara**  
Why did you send for me?

**Odile**  
Because I am afraid of being wrong in either direction. Call them persons and the assembly may take them from a farm that loves them. Call them stock and I have said exactly what the sale needs me to say. And I will not hand forty living creatures to a court on the strength of what a goat said in a barn.
At the far end of the byre an old nanny with a grey muzzle got up out of the straw, one leg at a time, and came the length of the floor. The others made room without being asked.

**Bracken**  
You are the one who listens. Sit. Sit down. Down in the straw.
Illuminara sat. It seemed to be the first item of business, and the sigh that went through the herd told her she had guessed right.

scenes.title: The Count
paragraphs: *The byre · the second evening*

Illuminara spent two evenings in the byre before she asked anyone anything. She had asked Odile to come without her clipboard, and Odile sat on an upturned bucket by the door with an expression somewhere between suspicion and relief.

She ate what the kids ate, which was oat cake pressed with something bitter and green, and found she liked it, and that the kids found her liking it very funny. She learned that the herd did not so much talk as take turns: one word, then a pause long enough to hold a whole thought, then another. She learned that a goat in conversation says the same thing three times, so that nobody has to ask twice. She had also noticed, without quite noticing, that every time one of the three phrases was spoken the whole herd leaned a little toward the east door.
At bedtime the kids played a game. One said a name, the next said it again and added another, and so on down the straw, and a small brown kid with one folded ear always got furthest.

**Tansy**  
Byre Gate. Split Ash. Byre Gate, Split Ash, the Wet Step. Byre Gate, Split Ash, the Wet Step, Tolly's Rise.

**Illuminara**  
What is the game called?

**Tansy**  
The count.
She said it the way a child says *the alphabet*. Illuminara sat very still, because something in her head had come loose and she did not want to knock it off the shelf.
*Not goats. Places.*

**Illuminara**  
Tansy, what comes after Tolly's Rise?

Fourteen names came out of the straw in order, ending at a place called the Long Look. The vet had written down three demands. They were one. The hill was where the rhyme went. The count was the rhyme. The going-up was the walking of it.

**Illuminara**  
Who taught you the count?

**Tansy**  
Bracken. Bracken's mother. Bracken's mother's mother. The count.

scenes.title: The Registry
paragraphs: *The Brannoch Dale registry, back room · the fourth morning*

The registrar listened to Odile without a word and then wheeled out a flat drawer. The enclosure award of 1844 was a map the colour of weak tea, and across the high ground ran a dotted line labelled in a hand like barbed wire: *Common Way, for the going-up and coming-down of beasts.* Fourteen waymarks were pencilled along it. Illuminara read them aloud, once, and Odile sat down on a box of ledgers.

**Odile**  
Split Ash. Tolly's Rise. My grandfather said that in the lambing shed. I thought it was a nursery rhyme.

**Illuminara**  
It is a survey. They have been walking the bounds of their own road for two hundred years and calling it a game, because nobody else was listening.

**Odile**  
Then why is it not in Pruett's title?

**Illuminara**  
The book says a right of common lapses if nobody claims it for twenty years. The herd walks the way every spring. But a goat cannot lodge a claim, so the book records no use.
The registrar slid a second sheet across the desk without comment. It was the sale particulars, offering the high pasture as an unencumbered single lot.

**Odile**  
So I claim the way for the holding, and the sale cannot close as written. But to do that I must say it is the holding's herd that uses it. Which is the word they did not want said. A thing people do to them.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. I could draft it tonight, and it would be correct, and it would win. I think we ask first.

**Odile**  
Ask whom?

**Illuminara**  
The people whose road it is.

scenes.title: The Correction
paragraphs: *The byre · that night*

She laid it out the slow way, a sentence and then a wait, for as long as it took. The way was in the award. The right belonged to the holding. The cooperative would claim it, the herd's going-up would stand as the use, and forty goats would keep the hill without anyone having to rule on what they were.
It was a good plan. She was a little proud of it, and had not hidden that well. Bracken heard it out to the end. Then she said, three times over, the word Illuminara had hoped not to hear.

**Bracken**  
No. No. No.

**Illuminara**  
Tell me where it is wrong.

**Bracken**  
For these forty. Forty die, the way is gone. Not for us. For the kids who are not yet. For whoever the herd is.

Illuminara's pride went out of her all at once, and what came in behind it was more useful. She had written the right for the animals in front of her. The herd had asked for a road that would outlast them.

**Illuminara**  
The right runs with the herd, whoever it is. Kids born, strays taken in. Not forty names.

**Bracken**  
Good. And a hill you are let on is a hill you are let on. We want the hearing. When the way changes, the cooperative counts us first. We say. We say before.

**Odile**  
You want a veto over my own land?

**Bracken**  
Over the road. Not the farm. The road is the road.
Odile looked at the old nanny for a long time. Then she looked at the straw, where Tansy lay asleep with her mouth still moving on the count.

**Odile**  
It means the cooperative can never sell the herd's road. Not in a bad year. Not ever.

**Bracken**  
No. And the way must be walked. Every spring. Kids at the front. If it is walked, it is used. If it is used, it is not lost. The hill remembers if we walk.

Illuminara wrote that down and understood what Bracken had just done. The right had lapsed once because nobody could claim it. It would never lapse again, because the claim was a morning walk that the herd would make whether or not anyone ever wrote it in a book.

scenes.title: The Gate
paragraphs: *The high pasture gate · afternoon, four days before the sitting*

Mr Hale Pruett was not a villain, which Illuminara found inconvenient. He was a tidy man in a waterproof the colour of porridge, with a client who had paid a deposit, a lender who wanted a clean title, and the look of someone who has read a great many documents carefully and is now being shown one that was not in the file. He had read the award twice.

**Pruett**  
You are asking my client to accept, for ever, forty goats walking through his scheme twice a year, on the strength of a nursery rhyme.

**Illuminara**  
On the strength of an award, which the rhyme matches stone by stone. I walked the line last night with my palm flat on the air. The old groove is still there under the gorse, four hundred years of the same weight on the same line.

**Pruett**  
The price falls.

**Illuminara**  
It does. And the way is in the award whether we tell your lender now or the lender's solicitor tells you in March. This way it is a four-metre lane along the Lamb Wall, outside the cabin plots, disclosed on the first day.

**Pruett**  
And if the goats change their minds?

**Illuminara**  
Then they say so, in the count, to the cooperative, before anything moves. It is the only change to that road you will ever have to deal with, and it will come with notice.
He looked up the hill for a while.

**Pruett**  
My guests will ask what the noise is.

**Illuminara**  
Twice a year, a fine one. Bring your lender to the walk.
He did not agree. He wrote *spring walk, autumn walk* in the margin of the particulars, which is how a careful man agrees without saying so.

scenes.title: The Going-Up
paragraphs: *The Common Way · dawn, the morning of the sitting*
They went up in the grey: forty goats, the whole membership of the cooperative and the registrar with a notebook, and Tansy at the front, because the kids go first.

**Tansy**  
Byre Gate, Split Ash, the Wet Step, Tolly's Rise, the Lamb Wall.

At the Wet Step she stopped, put one hoof in the water to prove it was wet, and went on, and forty animals lifted their feet over the same stones in the same order. A hollow the width of a goat ran through the gorse under the frost. Odile walked at the back with her hands in her pockets, saying the names under her breath and getting two of them wrong. Pruett had come, in the porridge-coloured waterproof, with his lender's number on his phone. At the Lamb Wall he stood and looked at the number and did not call it.

Illuminara walked last of all, and was surprised by how much she minded being last. She had decoded a rhyme and found a map and lost an argument to a goat, and none of it had felt like this: a hill being gone up by those it belonged to, one name at a time, at the speed of the smallest.
At the Long Look Bracken stopped, and the herd stopped behind her. The whole dale lay below them in the first sun with its roofs smoking.

**Bracken**  
Now the hill knows who is coming.

**Tansy**  
Again?

**Bracken**  
Again. Next spring. And the spring after.

scenes.title: What the Assembly Left Open
paragraphs: *Brannoch Dale assembly hall · noon*

The assembly's question was whether forty goats were livestock or residents, and it spent an hour discovering that it had not been asked the right one. Odile Marrick stood up with no notes. She said the cooperative was not asking for a category. It was claiming the Common Way in the award of 1844 for its holding, covenanting to hear the herd's chosen speakers before it changed anything, and filing that covenant at the registry with a hoof-print inked beside her signature, because Bracken had insisted on a mark.

The chair asked whether this decided what the goats were. Odile said it decided what they could count on. The assembly adjourned the other question, as she had hoped, and nobody much minded, since the hill was no longer for sale in the form that had made the question urgent. Pruett's client bought the lower meadow and the cabin plots with a lane written into the title, at a lower price and with a lender who asked only that the spring walk be put in the brochure.

It cost something. Two members of the cooperative resigned that week, one of them a man who had wanted the sale money and who would not forgive Odile for choosing the goats' road over his drains. The question of what the herd was remained open, and Bracken's speakers would have to defend the covenant at the count for years.

That night in the byre Tansy said the count, the whole fourteen, and did not lose a name. Illuminara found she was saying it with her, under her breath, the way and not the goats. Odile stood in the doorway with the cooperative's book and no clipboard, and when the last name was done she wrote under the date, in her small square hand, *Count taken.*

Illuminara sat. It seemed to be the first item of business, and the sigh that went through the herd told her she had guessed right.

scenes.title: The Count
paragraphs: *The byre · the second evening*

Illuminara spent two evenings in the byre before she asked anyone anything. She had asked Odile to come without her clipboard, and Odile sat on an upturned bucket by the door with an expression somewhere between suspicion and relief.

She ate what the kids ate, which was oat cake pressed with something bitter and green, and found she liked it, and that the kids found her liking it very funny. She learned that the herd did not so much talk as take turns: one word, then a pause long enough to hold a whole thought, then another. She learned that a goat in conversation says the same thing three times, so that nobody has to ask twice. She had also noticed, without quite noticing, that every time one of the three phrases was spoken the whole herd leaned a little toward the east door.
At bedtime the kids played a game. One said a name, the next said it again and added another, and so on down the straw, and a small brown kid with one folded ear always got furthest.

**Tansy**  
Byre Gate. Split Ash. Byre Gate, Split Ash, the Wet Step. Byre Gate, Split Ash, the Wet Step, Tolly's Rise.

**Illuminara**  
What is the game called?

**Tansy**  
The count.
She said it the way a child says *the alphabet*. Illuminara sat very still, because something in her head had come loose and she did not want to knock it off the shelf.
*Not goats. Places.*

**Illuminara**  
Tansy, what comes after Tolly's Rise?

Fourteen names came out of the straw in order, ending at a place called the Long Look. The vet had written down three demands. They were one. The hill was where the rhyme went. The count was the rhyme. The going-up was the walking of it.

**Illuminara**  
Who taught you the count?

**Tansy**  
Bracken. Bracken's mother. Bracken's mother's mother. The count.

scenes.title: The Registry
paragraphs: *The Brannoch Dale registry, back room · the fourth morning*

The registrar listened to Odile without a word and then wheeled out a flat drawer. The enclosure award of 1844 was a map the colour of weak tea, and across the high ground ran a dotted line labelled in a hand like barbed wire: *Common Way, as anciently used, for the going-up and coming-down of beasts to the common grazing above the Lamb Wall.* Fourteen waymarks were pencilled along it. Illuminara read them aloud, once, and Odile sat down on a box of ledgers.

**Odile**  
Split Ash. Tolly's Rise. My grandfather said that in the lambing shed. I thought it was a nursery rhyme.

**Illuminara**  
It is a survey. The award only wrote down a road that was already old. They have been saying the bounds of it since before the ink, and calling it a game, because nobody else was listening.

**Odile**  
Then why is it not in Pruett's title?

**Registrar**  
Because there are two ledgers. The award book keeps a right alive by an entry, and nothing else. A holder's claim is an entry. A walk that I or a holder sets down is an entry. Twenty years with none, and the right lapses. Pruett's title is drawn from the parcel index, and the index carries only what a holder has entered against a parcel. The last entry in the award book is nineteen years old, a lambing-week walk my predecessor happened to see. Nobody has ever entered the Way against the land.

**Illuminara**  
So the right is alive in one book and invisible in the other. The herd has kept the road alive on foot, and the paper has let it go quiet. Eleven months left on the clock.

**Registrar**  
And a goat cannot lodge a claim. The sale particulars were drawn from the index as it stands.
He slid a second sheet across the desk. It offered the high pasture as an unencumbered single lot.

**Odile**  
So I enter a claim for the holding, and the Way goes onto the title before the lot is divided, and the sale cannot close as written. But to do that I must say it is the holding's herd that uses it. Which is the word they did not want said. A thing people do to them.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. I could draft it tonight, and it would be correct, and it would win. I think we ask first.

**Odile**  
Ask whom?

**Illuminara**  
The people whose road it is.

scenes.title: The Correction
paragraphs: *The byre · that night*

She laid it out the slow way, a sentence and then a wait, for as long as it took. The way was in the award. The right belonged to the holding. The cooperative would claim it, the herd's going-up would stand as the use, and forty goats would keep the hill without anyone having to rule on what they were.
It was a good plan. She was a little proud of it, and had not hidden that well. Bracken heard it out to the end. Then she said, three times over, the word Illuminara had hoped not to hear.

**Bracken**  
No. No. No.

**Illuminara**  
Tell me where it is wrong.

**Bracken**  
For these forty. Forty die, the way is gone. Not for us. For the kids who are not yet. For whoever the herd is.

Illuminara's pride went out of her all at once, and what came in behind it was more useful. She had written the right for the animals in front of her. The herd had asked for a road that would outlast them.

**Illuminara**  
The right runs with the herd, whoever it is. Kids born, strays taken in. Not forty names.

**Bracken**  
Good. And a road to a shut gate is no road. The grass at the end of it is the end of the road. We want the hearing. When the way changes, the cooperative counts us first. We say. We say before.

**Odile**  
You want a veto over my own land?

**Bracken**  
Over the road. Not the farm. The road is the road.

**Odile**  
And where it goes?

**Bracken**  
A road goes somewhere.
Odile looked at the old nanny for a long time. Then she looked at the straw, where Tansy lay asleep with her mouth still moving on the count.

**Odile**  
Then the sale loses the top of the hill. The grass above the Lamb Wall stays in the cooperative's name, out of every lot, and I put that to people who voted for the whole of it. I will write more than you asked. Neither the Way nor the grass it goes to can ever be sold, and nothing on either is changed without your speakers heard first. Not in a bad year. Not ever.

**Bracken**  
That is more than we asked. Good. It is not enough. A road no one walks is a road in a drawer. The way must be walked. Every spring. Kids at the front. If it is walked and the book sees it, it is used. If it is used, it is not lost. The hill remembers if we walk.

Illuminara wrote that down and understood what Bracken had just done. The right had come within eleven months of lapsing because nobody could claim it. It would not come near again, because the entry was a morning walk the herd would make whether or not anyone asked, and the registrar had only to be there to see it.

scenes.title: The Gate
paragraphs: *The high pasture gate · afternoon, four days before the sitting*

Mr Hale Pruett was not a villain, which Illuminara found inconvenient. He was a tidy man in a waterproof the colour of porridge, acting for a buyer who had paid a deposit, with a lender who wanted a clean title behind her, and the look of someone who has read a great many documents carefully and is now being shown one that was not in the file. He had read the award twice.

**Pruett**  
You are asking my client to accept, for ever, forty goats walking through his scheme twice a year, on the strength of a nursery rhyme.

**Illuminara**  
On the strength of an award, which the rhyme matches stone by stone. I walked the line last night with my palm flat on the air. The old groove is still there under the gorse, four hundred years of the same weight on the same line.

**Pruett**  
And the lot is halved.

**Illuminara**  
It is. The grass above the Lamb Wall leaves the sale. Your client keeps the lower meadow, the road frontage, the water, and seven of his eleven plots. The Way is a four-metre lane along the wall, outside the plots, mapped and entered on the title on the first day instead of found by your lender's solicitor in March.

**Pruett**  
The price falls.

**Illuminara**  
It does. She will lend against a lane she can read. She cannot lend against a claim in the registrar's drawer that nobody has told her about.

**Pruett**  
And if the goats change their minds?

**Illuminara**  
Then they say so, in the count, to the cooperative, before anything moves. It is the only change to that lane you will ever have to deal with, and it will come with notice.
He looked up the hill for a while.

**Pruett**  
My guests will ask what the noise is.

**Illuminara**  
Twice a year, a fine one. Bring your lender to the walk.

**Pruett**  
I agree to nothing. I will carry a mapped lane, seven plots and a walk to my client, and they will say what they say.
He wrote *spring walk, autumn walk* in the margin of the particulars, which is how a careful man marks what he expects to have to defend.

scenes.title: The Going-Up
paragraphs: *The Common Way · dawn, the morning of the sitting*
They went up in the grey: forty goats, the whole membership of the cooperative and the registrar with a notebook, and Tansy at the front, because the kids go first.

**Tansy**  
Byre Gate, Split Ash, the Wet Step, Tolly's Rise, the Lamb Wall.

At the Wet Step she stopped, put one hoof in the water to prove it was wet, and went on, and forty animals lifted their feet over the same stones in the same order. A hollow the width of a goat ran through the gorse under the frost. Odile walked at the back with her hands in her pockets, saying the names under her breath and getting two of them wrong. The registrar walked beside the kids and wrote, after each waymark, a line.

Pruett had come, in the porridge-coloured waterproof, with his phone in his hand. At the Lamb Wall he stood and looked at it while the herd went past him, and then he read aloud, to nobody, a message that had come in at five.

**Pruett**  
From my client. Seven good plots and a story no other cabins in the county have, beats eleven plots and a lawsuit. Sign it.

He dialled the other number. Illuminara, last in the line, heard only his half, which was enough: *Yes. A registered lane. Seven plots. The ground above the wall out of the sale.* A long listening. *Forty. The kids go first.* Another. He laughed once, unwillingly.

**Pruett**  
She will lend against a lane on the title, not against a surprise. And she wants to know whether they walk on Sundays.

Illuminara walked last of all, and was surprised by how much she minded being last. She had decoded a rhyme and found a map and lost an argument to a goat, and none of it had felt like this: a hill being gone up by those it belonged to, one name at a time, at the speed of the smallest.

At the Long Look Bracken stopped, and the herd stopped behind her. The whole dale lay below them in the first sun with its roofs smoking, and the registrar closed his notebook on the first entry of the next twenty years.

**Bracken**  
Now the hill knows who is coming.

**Tansy**  
Again?

**Bracken**  
Again. Next spring. And the spring after.

scenes.title: What the Assembly Left Open
paragraphs: *Brannoch Dale assembly hall · noon*

The assembly's question was whether forty goats were livestock or residents, and it spent an hour discovering that it had not been asked the right one. Odile Marrick stood up with no notes. She said the cooperative was not asking for a category. It was claiming the Common Way in the award of 1844 for its holding, with that morning's walk entered in the award book as use and the claim entered against the title before the lot was divided. It was covenanting that neither the Way nor the grass it went to would ever be sold, and that nothing on either would change until the herd's chosen speakers had been heard. She had filed the covenant that morning, with a hoof-print inked beside her signature, because Bracken had insisted on a mark.

The chair asked whether this decided what the goats were. Odile said it decided what they could count on. The assembly adjourned the other question, as she had hoped, and nobody much minded, since the hill was no longer for sale in the form that had made the question urgent. The cooperative kept the high pasture above the Lamb Wall in its own name, and the herd would go on grazing it as it always had, on ground the cooperative had bound itself never to sell. Pruett's client signed the amendment at the gate before ten: the lower meadow and seven plots, at a lower price, with the lane along the wall written into the title as the Common Way, and a lender who asked only that the spring walk be put in the brochure.

It cost something. Two members of the cooperative resigned that week, one of them a man who had wanted the sale money and who would not forgive Odile for choosing the goats' road over his drains. The question of what the herd was remained open, and Bracken's speakers would have to defend the covenant at the count for years.

That night in the byre Tansy said the count, the whole fourteen, and did not lose a name. Illuminara found she was saying it with her, under her breath, the way and not the goats. Odile stood in the doorway with the cooperative's book and no clipboard, and when the last name was done she wrote under the date, in her small square hand, *Count taken.*
